transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-27 14:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Nina (Redwood), Liam (Quantaco), Riya (Quantaco infra), Marco (Quantaco PM), Sara (Quantaco security)

00:00 Speaker 1 (Sophie): All right folks, thanks for joining. Quick check in - can everyone see my screen?
00:07 Speaker 2 (Liam): Yep, looks good.
00:09 Sophie: Cool. Agenda: go over the tokens per dollar numbers from last week's run, dig into caching and batching tradeoffs, and decide on the 24 hour benchmark next steps. Diego, any quick notes before we jump in?
00:22 Diego: Yeah, just one thing - we changed the batch policy for the last run; I set max batch size to 64 for the A100 nodes and enabled continuous batching with a 10ms coalesce window. That changed throughput a bit vs the earlier job. Also turned on prefix cache for the top 20% of requests.
00:38 Marco: Top 20% meaning top frequency prompts, right?
00:41 Diego: Yeah, the most common prompt prefixes we saw in the sample set. It's not KV cache for session state, it's prefix-level caching - saves repeated attention/kv compute.
00:52 Speaker 3 (Riya): Quick question - when you say savings, is that measured in tokens or compute seconds? The spreadsheet shows both and I'm trying to reconcile.
01:00 Diego: Good call. On the sheet - we report tokens per second and tokens per dollar. The cache reduces effective tokens generated per model run because many tokens are served out of cache, so you see a jump in tokens/sec per dollar. But compute seconds drop too, obviously.
01:16 Liam: I was looking at the 8:1 improvement in one row - that feels high, is that real or an artifact of the test set?
01:24 Sophie: It's mostly because that set had a high prefix reuse rate. In prod distribution it will be lower; we estimated a conservatively lower ~2.2-3x for your workload based on the request histogram you shared.
01:36 Marco: Right, our product has lots of templated prompts so it's plausible. But what about latency impact when batching is bigger? We care about p95.
01:43 Diego: Exactly, there's the tradeoff. With max batch 64 we saw peak throughput improve ~30% but p95 latency moved from ~180ms to ~360ms on H100 equivalent perf. That's because batching introduces queueing delay; we can tune target latency vs cost.
01:58 Sophie: Let's pull up the 'cost-econ' sheet - (link shared) - Diego, can you talk through the tokens/sec per dollar curve you produced?
02:12 Diego: Sure. Column A lists model variants - gpt-xxl-16k-8bit, gpt-xxl-16k-fp16, smaller quantized 6bit variants. We ran them on H100 and A100 pools. The tokens/sec per dollar is normalized to a baseline of hosted API pricing for the 8-bit model. With prefix cache enabled you see a 1.8-3x effective improvement depending on prefix hit rate. Without cache you're much closer to baseline.
02:37 Liam: Are those numbers including infra amortization? Like reserved Dedicated vs on-demand?
02:42 Diego: We included raw GPU cost assumptions; the spreadsheet has two tabs - hosted per-token rate and dedicated reserved hourly cost breakdown. We can toggle to your committed pricing to see adjusted tokens/$ for reserved pools.
02:55 Sara: On security, quick note - the shared spreadsheet link is fine, but we need to ensure the bench data doesn't include customer PII. Please sanitize logs.
03:04 Sophie: Absolutely, we'll scrub logs. Diego - can you run the 24h bench with redacted traces?
03:09 Diego: Yep. We'll sample telemetry instead of full traces and mask IDs.
03:12 Marco: Back to batching - you mentioned continuous batching with 10ms coalesce. Can we try 5ms and 20ms to see the latency curve?
03:20 Diego: Yes, that's easy. We can parameter sweep coalesce window and max batch size. But note that reducing coalesce to 5ms reduces batch occupancy and hurts tokens/sec. It's a convex curve.
03:29 Liam: For our SLAs, p95 <= 250ms is important for some routes. So any batching config that pushes p95 > 250ms won't work for those routes.
03:38 Sophie: That's helpful; we should separate routes by latency sensitivity in the next run - route-level policies.
03:44 Diego: We can do per-route batching targets and route warm caching - prefix cache per route. That keeps high-throughput routes cheap while latency-sensitive ones use smaller batches or even dedicated low-latency nodes.
03:56 Riya: One more infra nuance - our dev cluster is in us-west-2 and we may need to colocate the dedicated fleet there. Do you have region-specific perf numbers?
04:05 Diego: perf differences are minimal across regions for H100 but network egress and routing can add latency; we included a regional column in the sheet with a ~2-12ms difference.
04:15 Liam: On quantization - the 6-bit models look cost-effective but I worry about quality regression. Did you do evals?
04:22 Diego: We ran baseline evals with your prompt set - rouge/accuracy and a small manual inspection. 6-bit shows minor delta in longer form completions; for Q&A routes it's within tolerance. We flagged any regressions in the model-evals tab.
04:34 Marco: Okay, so idea: use 6-bit for high-volume non-critical routes and 8-bit/fp16 for quality-sensitive ones.
04:40 Sophie: Exactly. That's part of the smart routing play - route to cheaper variant unless quality thresholds fail, then fall back.
04:47 Speaker 4 (Nina): Quick interjection - caching TTLs matter. If TTL is too short we lose hit-rate gains; too long and you might serve stale content. What's the TTL you used?
04:57 Diego: For the prefix cache run I used 5m for ephemeral prefixes and 24h for static templates. We can tune based on your content churn.
05:06 Alex (off): (inaudible)
05:08 Liam: Another question - tokens/sec per dollar numbers assume a certain prompt length distribution. We sent the histogram but can you walk me through how that affects numbers?
05:18 Diego: Sure. Average prompt length influences compute per request and batch fill. If your median prompt is 40 tokens vs 120 tokens, throughput and cost per completed response shift. The sheet has sensitivity scenarios for median length 30/60/120 tokens. For your distribution the conservative estimate is X tokens per req which maps to the 2.2-3x cache benefit.
05:36 Marco: For the 24h run can you also simulate peak windows - our traffic has 10x spikes at 10am PST sometimes.
05:44 Sophie: Good call. Diego, can you include a windowed spike test?
05:47 Diego: Yes, we'll run steady-state plus a 1h 10x spike to measure autoscaling and latency under load.
05:55 Riya: On autoscaling - how long to spin up extra nodes for Dedicated? We don't want cold-start blips hurting p95.
06:03 Diego: Our Dedicated autoscale policy uses pre-warmed spare capacity and fast provisioning - typical scale to new nodes within ~45-60s. But if you need hard p95 guarantees during spikes, we recommend reserved burst capacity or overprovisioning by X%.
06:17 Sara: Also need to log audit trails for scaling events, which are part of our compliance checklist. Are those available?
06:23 Sophie: Yes, audit logs are exportable; we'll include details in the security package.
06:27 Speaker 1 (Sophie): All right let's fast-forward to the key numbers from the spreadsheet - Diego, call out three concrete configs we think are interesting and the tokens/sec/$ numbers.
06:37 Diego: Config A: fp16 on H100, no prefix cache, max batch 32 -> baseline tokens/sec/$ = 1.0 (normalized). p95 ~180ms. Config B: 8-bit quant on A100, prefix cache hit ~35%, max batch 64 -> tokens/sec/$ = 2.5x, p95 ~350ms during steady state. Config C: 6-bit quant, prefix cache hit ~50%, route-level batching (latency zones) -> tokens/sec/$ = 3.4x, p95 for latency-sensitive route ~190ms, for bulk route ~420ms.
07:10 Liam: Those are useful. My ask: show per-route cost for three routes (search, summarization, chat) in the sheet so we can map to product pricing.
07:19 Sophie: We'll add that. Diego, also include a column for effective per-completion cost ($ per response) not just tokens.
07:26 Diego: Yep.
07:28 Marco: Any surprises from telemetry? Errors or timeouts?
07:31 Diego: Small rate of OOM on a few 16k sequences on the 6-bit model when we tried large batch sizes; we added early rejection for >12k seqs to avoid. Also KV cache warmup caused a short tail in latency on cold starts.
07:45 Liam: Hmm - we do have some long-form generation routes. If early rejection is necessary, can Redwood return a suggested fallback like trimming context or offloading to larger nodes?
07:55 Diego: Yup, we have policies to truncate context or route to a larger memory node; we can implement transparent fallbacks.
08:02 Sophie: OK, circling next steps: 24 hour run, per-route pricing, spike window test, and security package. Anything else?
08:09 Sara: Please include KMS/HSM integration options and whether you support customer-managed keys on Private deployment.
08:14 Sophie: We'll include that in the package.
08:16 Diego: One small thing - for the 24h run we'd like you to confirm which routes are latency sensitive vs cost sensitive so we can label them in the run.
08:25 Liam: I'll share a single doc with route names and desired p95.
08:29 Sophie: Great. Any final questions?
08:32 Marco: Just timeline - when can we expect the updated spreadsheet and benchmark?
08:36 Sophie: We'll run the benchmark overnight and aim to share results by EOD Friday 8/28 plus updated cost-econ sheet.
08:44 Diego: And we'll drop the raw telemetry (sanitized) into the shared folder and post links in the CRM.
08:49 Sophie: Perfect. Thanks everyone - we'll follow up in Slack with the schedule for the deep-dive next Tuesday.
08:55 Liam: Thanks all.
09:00 Meeting end.

Notes about transcript: imperfect auto-transcription present; some names and acronyms may be misrecognized (e.g., H100/H-100, KV cache spelled K V cache in places). References: cost-econ spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/qai-cost-econ), security package (link: https://redwood.example.com/security/qai-package).
